figureFiles.caption: The House Sparrow, American Robin and American Crow drawn to the same scale, at the middle of each species’ length range. A crow is nearly twice a robin’s length and nearly three times a sparrow’s, which makes these three good yardsticks.
Six common shape families recognized without any color: by bill shape, neck and leg length, posture, or the outline of wings and tail. Not to scale.

The standard names for the parts of a songbird. The wing bars are pale tips on two rows of wing coverts; the supercilium runs above the eye, and the malar stripe runs back from the base of the lower mandible.

lesson.hook: In April 1934, a 25-year-old art teacher at a school near Boston published a slim book that several publishers had already turned down. His publisher, Houghton Mifflin, printed just 2,000 copies and paid him no royalties on the first thousand. The printing sold out within weeks. The teacher was Roger Tory Peterson, and the book was *A Field Guide to the Birds*. Its idea was simple and new: you do not need a bird in your hand to name it. You need to know the few visible marks that separate it from every similar bird, and where and when it lives. More than ninety years later, field guides and identification apps still build on that idea. This chapter teaches you the method behind it, one step at a time.
lesson.overview: This chapter turns the anatomy of the first three chapters into a practical skill: naming the bird in front of you. You will learn the order in which experienced birders gather evidence. First comes size and shape, which usually tells you the family (the level of classification Chapter 1 told you to learn first). Then come field marks, read with the standard names for the parts of a bird, which build on the feather groups of Chapter 1. Then come behavior, habitat, range and season, where the wing shapes and flight styles of Chapter 2 and the bills of Chapter 3 earn their keep. The last section shows how field guides are organized and how to keep a checklist, the record you will submit in Chapter 8. Identifying birds by ear waits for Chapter 5.
objectives: Estimate a bird’s size against reference birds and place it in a shape family from its silhouette.
Name the main parts of a songbird and use field marks to separate similar species.
Use behavior, habitat, range and season to narrow the candidates and test an identification.
Find a species in a field guide, read its range map, and keep a complete checklist of the birds you see.

sections.title: Size and shape first
reading: Most beginners look at a new bird’s color first. Experienced birders start somewhere else. The Cornell Lab of Ornithology teaches four keys to identification, in this order: size and shape, color pattern, behavior, and habitat [1]. Size and shape come first for good reasons. You can judge them in poor light, against the sky, or at a distance where color disappears, and they change far less than plumage does with sex, age and season. Shape also usually tells you the bird’s family, and as Chapter 1 showed, knowing the family narrows thousands of possible species to a handful [1, 3]. The Cornell Lab’s own example makes the point: an Evening Grosbeak (*Coccothraustes vespertinus*) and an American Goldfinch (*Spinus tristis*) are both yellow, black and white, but the grosbeak is far larger and has a much thicker bill [1].

Size is harder to judge than it sounds, because a bird alone in a tree or in the sky has nothing to compare it with. The cure is a set of **reference birds** you know well. Three common North American species make a good yardstick. A House Sparrow (*Passer domesticus*) is 15–17 cm long, a little shorter than a new pencil. An American Robin (*Turdus migratorius*), the running example of this book, is 20–28 cm. An American Crow (*Corvus brachyrhynchos*) is 40–53 cm, nearly twice a robin’s length [2]. A Rock Pigeon (*Columba livia*), at 30–36 cm, fills the gap between robin and crow [2]. Figure 4.1 draws the first three to scale. Describe a new bird in these terms: “a bit bigger than a sparrow,” “robin-sized,” “smaller than a crow.”

Field guides give a bird’s **length** from the tip of the bill to the tip of the tail, measured with the bird stretched out [4]. A living bird hunches its neck and tilts its tail, so it looks shorter than its listed length. Weather changes apparent size too: a sparrow fluffed against the cold looks plumper than the same bird on a summer afternoon, because it is trapping warm air in its feathers, the insulation you met in Chapters 1 and 3. Size judged against a bird standing next to the mystery bird is reliable; size judged against your memory of a bird is not.

Shape is a set of proportions, which Kenn Kaufman and other guide authors call **structure** [3]. Look at the bill: its length compared with the head, and its form, whether a seed-cracking cone, a thin insect-picking tweezer, a hook or a flat duck bill (Chapter 3 explained what each does). Look at the size of the head, the length of the neck and legs, the length and tip shape of the tail (notched, square or rounded), and the wings, short and rounded or long and pointed (Chapter 2). Posture matters as well: a robin stands fairly upright on a lawn, a woodpecker clings upright to bark, braced on its stiff tail. Figure 4.2 shows six common families that can be named from outline alone.

Proportions often settle cases that plumage cannot. Downy Woodpeckers (*Dryobates pubescens*) and Hairy Woodpeckers (*Dryobates villosus*) are both black and white with a white stripe down the back. The Downy is smaller, 14–17 cm against 18–26 cm, but size is hard to judge on a lone bird [2]. The better test is the bill: the Downy’s is clearly shorter than its head, while the Hairy’s is about as long as the head [2]. Small hawks give the same lesson. Female Sharp-shinned Hawks (*Accipiter striatus*) are about a third larger than males, which brings them close to the size of a male Cooper’s Hawk, so experienced observers rely on structure instead: Cooper’s Hawks have a larger head and a rounded tail tip, Sharp-shinned Hawks a smaller head and a square-tipped tail [2].

Birders also speak of a bird’s **jizz** (also written GISS), the overall impression of size, shape and movement that lets an expert name a distant bird at a glance. The word is slang and its origin is uncertain, but the skill is real: it is shape and size, absorbed through practice until you no longer notice you are using them. Treat your first impression as a hypothesis. The next sections show how field marks, behavior and context test it.

keyTerms.def: A familiar species, such as a House Sparrow, American Robin or American Crow, used as a yardstick for judging the size of an unknown bird.
The distance from the tip of the bill to the tip of the tail, as given in field guides.
A bird’s proportions: the relative size and shape of its bill, head, neck, wings, tail and legs.
A bird’s outline without color, which is often enough to name its family.
Birders’ slang for the overall impression of size, shape and movement that lets experienced observers recognize a bird quickly.

example.title: Worked example: Downy or Hairy at the suet feeder
steps: Shape first. A black-and-white bird clings upright to a suet cage, propped on its tail, and hammers with a straight, chisel-like bill. That posture and bill put it in the woodpecker family.

Size against a reference bird. A House Sparrow lands on the same feeder. The woodpecker is about the sparrow’s length, not obviously bigger. That fits a Downy (14–17 cm) better than a Hairy (18–26 cm), but treat it as a clue, not proof.
Structure. The bill is short, clearly shorter than the head is long from front to back. On a Hairy Woodpecker the bill would be about as long as the head.

Look for a second, independent mark. When the bird flicks its tail, the white outer tail feathers show black spots. Downy Woodpeckers usually have these spots; Hairy Woodpeckers usually have plain white outer tail feathers.
Conclusion: a Downy Woodpecker. Three separate lines of evidence (size against a sparrow, bill-to-head proportion, tail spots) all point the same way.
example.takeaway: Proportions measured against the bird itself, such as bill length compared with head length, are more reliable than a guess at absolute size.

misconception.myth: Color is the first thing to look at, because that is what makes each bird different.
misconception.fact: Color changes with light, distance, sex, age, season and molt, and many unrelated birds share the same colors. Size and shape are visible in almost any light and usually tell you the family, which is why the Cornell Lab’s method starts there. Color pattern comes next, to separate species within the family.

practice.q: You see an unfamiliar bird on a fence post. Which is the most reliable way to judge its size?
choices: Estimate its length in centimeters from memory
Judge size by how bright its colors are
Compare it with a familiar bird perched nearby, such as a sparrow or robin
Judge size by how loud its call is
practice.explanation: Absolute size is easy to misjudge, especially at a distance or against the sky. A familiar reference bird next to the unknown one gives a direct comparison. Color and loudness say little about size.

practice.q: A small hawk is perched on your feeder pole. A friend says, “It’s big, so it must be a Cooper’s Hawk.” Explain why size alone cannot settle this, and name two features of shape you would check instead.
practice.answer: Female Sharp-shinned Hawks are about a third larger than males and approach the size of a male Cooper’s Hawk, so a large-looking bird could be either species. Check the tail tip (rounded in Cooper’s, square in Sharp-shinned) and the size of the head relative to the body (larger in Cooper’s, smaller in Sharp-shinned).
practice.explanation: A good answer mentions the size overlap between female Sharp-shinned and male Cooper’s Hawks and gives two structural marks, such as tail-tip shape and head size.

practice.q: Which silhouette feature tells you most clearly that a bird is a woodpecker?
choices: It clings upright to a tree trunk, braced on its stiff tail
It is black and white
It has a red patch on its head
It is about the size of a robin
practice.explanation: Clinging upright with the tail used as a prop is a shape-and-posture trait of the woodpecker family. Many birds are black and white or robin-sized, and plenty of non-woodpeckers have red on the head.

sections.title: Field marks and bird topography
reading: A **field mark** is a visible feature that helps tell one species from similar ones: a stripe over the eye, bars on the wing, spots on the tail, a patch of color on the rump. Peterson built his 1934 guide around this idea. Instead of describing every feather, he showed similar species together and pointed out only the marks that separate them, an approach he called identification by elimination, combining field marks with knowledge of range [1]. His later guides became famous for small arrows pointing straight at the marks that matter. Every modern guide, from Sibley’s paintings to photographic guides, still works this way [2].

To use field marks you need words for where they are. Birders and ornithologists share a standard vocabulary for the outside of a bird, called **bird topography** (Figure 4.3). On the head, the **crown** is the top, the forehead is in front of it and the **nape** is the back of the neck. The **lores** are the small area between the eye and the bill. A stripe above the eye is the **supercilium**, or eyebrow; a ring of feathers around the eye is an eye-ring. A dark stripe running back from the base of the lower bill, between the cheek and the throat, is a **malar stripe**. The bill has an upper and a lower **mandible** [2, 3].

The body divides into upperparts and underparts. Above are the back, the **rump** just in front of the tail, and the tail itself. Below are the throat, breast, belly, the **flanks** along the sides under the folded wing, and the **undertail coverts**, the feathers that cover the base of the tail from below. On a perched bird the folded wing shows rows of covert feathers overlapping like roof shingles. When the coverts of two rows have pale tips, they form two pale lines across the wing, the **wing bars**. Behind them lie the **tertials**, the innermost flight feathers, and at the wingtip the primaries, the remiges you met in Chapter 1 [2, 3].

Now read a familiar bird with these words. An adult American Robin has a blackish-gray head with white arcs above and below the eye, a broken eye-ring rather than a complete one. The bill is yellow. The throat is white with dark streaks, the breast warm orange, and the lower belly and undertail coverts white. The back and wings are gray-brown, with no wing bars. Females are usually paler than males, but the two overlap [4]. Each item in that description names a part, so anyone with a field guide can check it.

Field marks matter most when two species look alike, and the best marks are often about pattern and where color sits rather than the exact shade. Male House Finches (*Haemorhous mexicanus*) have red mostly on the head, breast and rump, with brown streaks on the flanks. Male Purple Finches (*Haemorhous purpureus*) look as if they were dipped in raspberry juice: the pinkish-red washes over the back and wings too, and the flanks lack distinct streaks. Females are easier still. A female Purple Finch has a whitish stripe over the eye and a dark stripe running back from the bill, framing a brown cheek; a female House Finch has a plain brown face [5].

Field marks vary, so never rely on just one. Males and females often differ, as in the finches. Young birds differ from adults; a juvenile robin has a spotted breast. Many species change plumage between breeding and nonbreeding seasons, and molt and feather wear change a bird’s appearance through the year, as Chapter 1 described [3]. Light matters too: the same red can look orange in low sun or brown in shade. A guide shows a typical bird in good light. Your bird may differ in small ways, and the marks that separate it from its look-alikes are the ones to check.

keyTerms.def: A visible feature, such as an eyebrow stripe, wing bar or tail spot, that helps separate one species from similar ones.
The standard set of names for the external parts of a bird, used to describe where field marks are.
A stripe of contrasting color running above the eye; birders often call it the eyebrow.
A stripe running back from the base of the lower mandible, between the cheek and the throat.
A pale line across the folded wing formed by pale tips on a row of wing coverts.
The feathers covering the base of the tail from below.

example.title: Worked example: describing a robin in the right words
steps: Start at the head. Crown and nape blackish-gray. White arcs above and below the eye: a broken eye-ring. Bill yellow.
Move down the front. Throat white with dark streaks. Breast warm orange. Lower belly and undertail coverts white.
Check the upperparts and wing. Back and wings plain gray-brown. No wing bars.
Add size and structure from Section 4.1. Robin-sized by definition: 20–28 cm, plump, with a medium-length tail and a straight bill.

Write it as one note: “Thrush-shaped, robin-sized; dark head with broken white eye-ring; yellow bill; streaked white throat; orange breast; white undertail coverts; plain gray-brown wings.” Every phrase names a part of Figure 4.3, so a reader can check it point by point.
example.takeaway: Naming the parts turns a vague impression (“orange bird”) into a description that someone else can check against a guide.

misconception.myth: If a bird doesn’t look exactly like the picture in my guide, it must be a different species or a rarity.
misconception.fact: Individual birds vary with sex, age, season, molt, feather wear and light, and a guide can show only typical birds. Check the specific marks that separate the species from its look-alikes. Most birds that look a little off are ordinary birds in an unusual plumage or light.

practice.q: What forms the wing bars on a perched songbird?
choices: Pale edges on the primaries
Pale tips on rows of wing coverts
White feathers on the flanks
Pale edges on the tail feathers
practice.explanation: Wing bars are lines across the folded wing made by pale tips on the coverts. The primaries are at the wingtip, the flanks are on the body, and the tail is behind the wing.

practice.q: A brown, streaky finch with a thick bill visits your feeder. Its face is plain brown, with no stripe over the eye, and its breast has long, thin, blurry streaks. Is it more likely a female House Finch or a female Purple Finch? Explain using field marks.
practice.answer: A female House Finch. Female Purple Finches have a bold face pattern, a whitish stripe over the eye and a dark stripe back from the bill framing a brown cheek, while female House Finches have a plain brown face. The long, thin, blurry breast streaks also fit a House Finch better than the short, thick, smudged streaks of a Purple Finch.
practice.explanation: A good answer names the face pattern (supercilium and dark stripe in Purple Finch, plain face in House Finch) as the deciding mark.

practice.q: A field guide says a warbler has “yellow lores.” Where should you look?
choices: On the top of the head
On the feathers under the tail
On the patch above the tail
Between the eye and the bill
practice.explanation: The lores are the small area between the eye and the base of the bill. The top of the head is the crown, the feathers under the tail are the undertail coverts, and the area just above the tail is the rump.

sections.title: Behavior, habitat, range and season
reading: How a bird moves is often as telling as how it looks. An American Robin on a lawn runs a few steps, stops abruptly, and often stares at the ground with its head cocked to one side before it lunges for a worm [1]. A White-breasted Nuthatch (*Sitta carolinensis*) climbs down tree trunks headfirst, which no woodpecker does; woodpeckers hitch upward, propped on their tails [1]. An Eastern Phoebe (*Sayornis phoebe*) pumps its tail down and up as it perches [1]. You can learn these habits from a distance, long before you can see a single field mark.

Flight behavior connects directly to Chapter 2. A Turkey Vulture (*Cathartes aura*) soars with its wings raised in a shallow V, a shape called a **dihedral**, rarely flaps, and teeters from side to side as it rides the air. A Red-tailed Hawk (*Buteo jamaicensis*) soars on flat wings [1]. On a distant bird with no visible color, the angle of the wings can be all you need. Hovering, which you studied in Chapter 2, works the same way: a bird that hangs in front of a flower on a blur of wings is almost certainly a hummingbird.

**Habitat** is the kind of place a bird lives, and most species are faithful to theirs. The Cornell Lab’s example is the Killdeer (*Charadrius vociferus*), a plover that runs about on open, grassy ground, often far from water [2]. Woodpeckers need trees, ducks need water, and marsh birds need marshes. Habitat is a guide rather than a rule, because migrants turn up in odd places when they stop to rest and feed (Chapter 7). A bird in the wrong habitat is worth a second look, not an automatic dismissal.

**Range** and **season** tell you which species are possible at all. A field guide’s range map shows where each species breeds, winters and passes through. The Ruby-throated Hummingbird (*Archilochus colubris*) is the only hummingbird that breeds in eastern North America [1], so a hummingbird in an Ohio garden in July is almost certainly that species before you see a feather. Season can mislead as well as help. Many American Robins do not migrate at all. In winter they gather in roaming flocks, eat fruit and roost in trees, so they vanish from lawns; robins have been reported in January in every U.S. state except Hawaii [3]. The “first robin of spring” is often a local bird that has switched back to defending a territory on a lawn [3].

Put the clues together the way a detective weighs evidence. The Cornell Lab advises keeping a running mental list of the birds most likely in your place and season [2]. Common birds are common, so a rare species needs stronger evidence than a familiar one. Three tests show that an identification is right. First, several independent lines of evidence agree: size, shape, pattern, behavior, habitat, range and season. Second, you have ruled out each look-alike with a specific mark, not just matched a picture. Third, the record can be checked by someone else, through notes, a sketch, a photograph or a recording. eBird, the online checklist program you will meet in Section 4.4, applies the same logic: reports that are unusual for the place and date are flagged and reviewed by experienced local birders before the data are used [4].

keyTerms.def: The kind of place where a species lives, such as forest, marsh, grassland or open water.
A map showing where a species occurs, usually separated into breeding, winter, year-round and migration areas.
Wings held raised above the body in a shallow V while soaring, as in the Turkey Vulture.
A species, or a population, that stays in the same area in all seasons rather than migrating.
A bird found far outside the normal range of its species.

example.title: Worked example: a hummingbird in Ohio, in July and in December
steps: Shape and behavior: a tiny bird with a needle-thin bill hovers at a feeder on a blur of wings. That places it among the hummingbirds before you see any color.
Range and season: the place is Ohio and the month is July. The Ruby-throated Hummingbird is the only hummingbird that breeds in eastern North America, so it is by far the most likely species.
Field marks: in good light an adult male shows a glowing red throat. A female or young bird lacks the red throat, but range and season have already made Ruby-throated the strong favorite.

Now change one fact: the same bird visits in December. Ruby-throated Hummingbirds have left for Central America by then. The usual answer no longer fits, so the bird could be a vagrant from the West, and it deserves photographs and a report.
Conclusion: in July, Ruby-throated Hummingbird; in December, an unknown hummingbird that needs field marks and documentation before anyone names it.
example.takeaway: Range and season decide which species to expect; field marks and evidence must carry the identification when the expected answer does not fit.

misconception.myth: All robins fly south for the winter, so the first robin you see in spring has just returned.
misconception.fact: Many American Robins stay through the winter across much of the United States. They form flocks, eat fruit and roost in trees, so they disappear from lawns. The spring robin on your lawn is often a local bird that has switched from flocking to defending a territory.

practice.q: A large dark bird soars over a field with its wings held in a shallow V, rocking from side to side and hardly flapping. Which species does this behavior fit best?
choices: Red-tailed Hawk
Turkey Vulture
American Crow
Rock Pigeon
practice.explanation: Soaring on raised wings (a dihedral) while teetering side to side is the classic flight of the Turkey Vulture. Red-tailed Hawks soar on flat wings, and crows and pigeons flap far more and do not soar this way.

practice.q: Someone reports a bird species that has never been recorded in your county, seen for two seconds in flight, with no photo. Using the three tests from this section, explain what would make you accept or doubt the record.
practice.answer: I would ask whether several independent features were seen and agree (size, shape, pattern, behavior, habitat, and whether range and season make it at all plausible), whether each similar species was ruled out by a specific mark, and whether there is evidence another person can check, such as notes, a sketch, a photo or a recording. A two-second view with no documentation of a species far out of range fails most of these tests, so I would treat it as unconfirmed rather than wrong.
practice.explanation: A strong answer uses all three tests (converging evidence, ruling out look-alikes, checkable documentation) and notes that rare birds need stronger evidence than common ones.

practice.q: A bird is climbing headfirst down the trunk of an oak. What is it most likely to be?
choices: A woodpecker
A Brown Creeper
A nuthatch
A hawk
practice.explanation: Nuthatches climb down trunks headfirst. Woodpeckers and Brown Creepers climb upward, propped on their stiff tails, and hawks do not climb trunks at all.

sections.title: Using a field guide and a checklist
reading: Peterson’s 1934 guide was small enough to carry and arranged for use outdoors. Similar species were drawn side by side in the same pose, and the text described only the marks and ranges that separate them [1, 2]. Its success, and the many editions that followed, helped turn bird watching from the hobby of a few naturalists into a popular pastime [5]. Modern guides, including David Sibley’s and Kenn Kaufman’s, follow the same plan with better art, photographs, range maps and far more plumages [3].

Most field guides arrange species in **taxonomic order**, the sequence of the official checklist, which keeps relatives together [3]. North American guides usually begin with ducks and geese and end with the songbirds, the passerines of Chapter 1. This is why learning families pays off: once you know that a bird is a woodpecker or a finch, you can turn straight to that section and compare all its members on facing pages. Use the index for names, and the illustrated quick-reference pages many guides include to find a family by shape.

Each species account repays a careful read. The illustrations show the plumages you are likely to meet (male and female, adult and young, breeding and nonbreeding) and often point out the key marks with labels or arrows. The text adds size, voice, habitat and behavior. The range map shows where the species breeds, winters, lives year-round and passes through on migration, usually in different colors; check each guide’s key, because the colors differ between guides [3]. Illustrated guides show an idealized bird with every mark visible; photographic guides show real birds, in whatever light the photographer had. Apps such as the Cornell Lab’s free Merlin suggest species from a photo or a recording. Treat their suggestions the way you treat your own first impression: as a hypothesis to test with the method of this chapter.

Keep **field notes**, and write before you look at the book. Record the date, time, place, habitat and weather, then describe the bird part by part with the vocabulary of Section 4.2, and add a rough sketch, however crude. Notes made before you open a guide record what you saw; notes made after tend to record what the picture showed. Good notes are also the evidence that lets someone else check an identification, the third test in Section 4.3.

A **checklist** is a list of the species you identified on one outing, with numbers. eBird, launched in 2002 by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and the National Audubon Society, collects such lists from birders worldwide [4]. Each checklist records the place, date, start time, duration, distance traveled and number of observers, and asks whether you are reporting every species you identified. A **complete checklist** answers yes. That matters to science: if a complete list from a marsh in May lacks a species, the species was probably not detected there, so researchers can measure absence as well as presence and correct for effort [4]. In Chapter 8 you will submit a standardized count of your own.

keyTerms.def: A portable book or app that helps identify species in the field by showing similar species together with their distinguishing marks and ranges.
The sequence in which species appear in an official checklist, which keeps related species and families together.
A written record, ideally with a sketch, of what you saw, made at the time and before consulting a guide.
A list of the species, with numbers, identified at one place on one outing.
A checklist that reports every species the observer identified, which allows scientists to infer that unreported species were not detected.

example.title: Worked example: from feeder to checklist
steps: Write first. “Saturday, 8:15–8:45 a.m., backyard feeder. Three sparrow-sized birds with thick, conical bills. Two males: red on head, breast and rump; brown streaks on flanks; back brown. One female: plain brown face, blurry streaks below.”
Find the family. The conical bill and size say finch. In a taxonomically arranged guide, the finches are near the back, among the songbirds.
Compare the facing plates. The Purple Finch male is washed with raspberry red on the back and lacks flank streaks; the female has a white eyebrow. Your notes match House Finch on both sexes.
Check the range map. House Finches live year-round across most of the United States, so the bird is expected here.

Record it. Enter “House Finch, 3” along with every other species you identified in those 30 minutes, give the start time, duration and distance (zero for a stationary count), and mark the checklist complete only if nothing you identified was left off.
example.takeaway: Notes written before opening the guide, compared against the right family pages and a range map, become a record that others can check and scientists can use.

misconception.myth: If an identification app names the bird, the identification is done.
misconception.fact: Apps give suggestions based on probability and pattern matching, and they can be wrong when a photo is blurry, a recording is noisy, or the bird is unusual. A suggestion is a hypothesis. It becomes an identification when the bird’s size, shape, field marks, behavior, range and season all agree with it and the look-alikes have been ruled out.

practice.q: Why does a field guide put the Downy Woodpecker, Hairy Woodpecker and Northern Flicker within a few pages of one another?
choices: They are all black and white
The guide is arranged in taxonomic order, which keeps members of the same family together
They are arranged by size
They all live in the same state
practice.explanation: Most guides follow the taxonomic order of an official checklist, so all woodpeckers (family Picidae) appear together. The flicker is mostly brown, not black and white, and the three are not grouped by size or state.

practice.q: When should you mark an eBird checklist as complete?
choices: When you saw at least ten species
When you have a photo of every bird
When you reported every species you were able to identify
When you birded for at least an hour
practice.explanation: A complete checklist means every species you identified is on the list. It does not depend on how many species you saw, how long you birded, or whether you photographed them.

practice.q: A friend’s notes read: “Saw a brown bird in the park. Pretty sure it was a sparrow.” Rewrite these as useful field notes, listing what should have been recorded.
practice.answer: Useful notes would include the date, time, exact place and habitat (for example, brushy edge of a pond), and weather; size against a reference bird; shape (bill form, tail length and shape, posture); field marks named by topography (crown stripes, supercilium, malar stripe, breast streaks or a central spot, wing bars); behavior (feeding on the ground, flicking the tail); any call or song; how long and how close the view was; and a rough sketch.
practice.explanation: A good answer covers when and where, size and shape, named field marks, behavior and the quality of the view, so that someone else could check the identification.

interactives.title: Body lengths of reference birds
interactives.intro: Lengths are bill tip to tail tip, at the middle of each species’ published range. Find the three yardstick birds (sparrow, robin, crow), then place each other bird between them.

items.label: Downy Woodpecker
items.note: 14–17 cm; sparrow-sized, unlike the larger Hairy Woodpecker (18–26 cm).

items.label: American Robin
items.note: 20–28 cm; the middle yardstick and our running example.

items.label: American Crow
items.note: 40–53 cm; the large yardstick, nearly twice a robin.

items.label: Mallard
items.note: 50–65 cm; a large duck, still much smaller than a Canada Goose.

items.label: Great Blue Heron
items.note: 97–137 cm; much of that length is neck and bill; the long legs are not counted.

interactives.title: Which shape family?
interactives.intro: Sort each bird by its silhouette and posture, not its color. Two items are traps; read the explanations.

items.why: A thrush: perches and hops, slim straight bill, medium tail, short legs.
A finch: sparrow-sized songbird with a thick, conical seed-cracking bill.
A songbird with a crest and a heavy conical bill. Its red color says nothing about its family.
A trap. It climbs trunks like a woodpecker, but it is a songbird with a short tail that it does not use as a prop, and it climbs headfirst down.
Clings upright, braced on stiff tail feathers, with a chisel-like bill.
A trap. Flickers often feed on the ground and are mostly brown, but their bill, stiff tail and clinging posture are a woodpecker’s.
Flat bill, sits low on the water, short legs.
Hooked bill, broad wings and a short fanned tail when soaring.
A small hawk, but still hooked-billed, with short rounded wings and a long tail for chasing birds through trees.

interactives.title: Mystery bird over the hayfield
interactives.intro: A July afternoon over farmland in central Pennsylvania. A large dark bird circles low over a hayfield. You have about a minute and no camera. Answer each question before you reveal it.

steps.q: Size and shape: it is clearly bigger than the crows nearby, with long, broad wings and a small head. Which groups does that suggest, and which does it rule out?
steps.a: A large soaring bird: a vulture, an eagle or a large hawk. Songbirds, woodpeckers, ducks and small forest hawks are ruled out by size and wing shape. Broad wings for soaring were the subject of Chapter 2.

steps.q: Behavior: the wings are held above the body in a shallow V, and the bird rocks from side to side, hardly flapping. Which candidate does this fit?
steps.a: The Turkey Vulture. Red-tailed Hawks soar on flat wings. Golden Eagles may lift their wings slightly but are larger and do not teeter the way vultures do.

steps.q: Field marks: from below, the flight feathers look silvery-pale against the dark front half of the wing, and the head is small and bare. Does this agree?
steps.a: Yes. A two-toned underwing (dark in front, paler flight feathers behind) and a small featherless head are standard marks of the Turkey Vulture, and they are independent of the flight behavior, so the two lines of evidence reinforce each other.

steps.q: Range, season and look-alikes: what else could it be in Pennsylvania in July, and how would you rule it out?
steps.a: The Black Vulture also lives in Pennsylvania. It has a short tail, white patches near the wingtips, and flies with bursts of quick flaps. Golden Eagles occur in the East mainly in migration and winter. With shape, behavior, field marks, range and season all agreeing and the look-alikes excluded, the answer is a Turkey Vulture.

interactives.title: Put the method in order
interactives.intro: Arrange the steps in the order this chapter teaches, from first look to finished record.
steps: Judge size against a reference bird
Read the shape and place the bird in a family
Note field marks, named by topography
Watch behavior and note the habitat
Check range and season in a field guide
Rule out each look-alike and record the evidence on a checklist
interactives.explain: Size and shape come first because they work at a distance and usually give the family. Field marks then separate species within the family. Behavior, habitat, range and season test the answer against what is likely, and ruling out look-alikes with recorded evidence is what makes the identification checkable.

slides.title: Chapter 4: Field identification
bullets: Size and shape first
Field marks and bird topography
Behavior, habitat, range and season
Field guides and checklists
slides.notes: Today we learn a method, not a list of birds. The same four steps work on a sparrow in your yard and a hawk over a ridge.

slides.title: Peterson’s idea (1934)
bullets: You do not need the bird in your hand
Show look-alikes side by side
Point out only the marks that separate them
Combine field marks with range
slides.notes: Peterson’s first printing of 2,000 copies sold out within weeks. Modern guides and apps still build on his identification by elimination.

slides.title: Size: use reference birds
bullets: House Sparrow 15–17 cm
American Robin 20–28 cm
American Crow 40–53 cm
Length is bill tip to tail tip; perched birds look shorter
slides.notes: Use Figure 4.1. Encourage students to describe birds as “sparrow-sized” or “between robin and crow” rather than guessing centimeters.

slides.title: Shape: structure and silhouette
bullets: Bill shape and length compared with the head
Tail length and tip shape
Wing shape (Chapter 2) and leg length
Posture: perching, clinging, swimming, wading
slides.notes: Figure 4.2 shows six families named from outline alone. The Downy and Hairy Woodpeckers show that a bill-to-head proportion can beat a guess at size.

slides.title: Field marks
bullets: Visible features that separate similar species
Pattern and position matter more than exact shade
Check more than one mark
Plumage varies with sex, age, season, molt and light
slides.notes: The finch pair is the classic example: where the red sits, and whether the flanks are streaked, matters more than how red the bird is.

slides.title: Bird topography
bullets: Head: crown, nape, lores, supercilium, eye-ring, malar stripe
Upperparts: back, rump, tail
Wing: coverts, wing bars, tertials, primaries
Underparts: throat, breast, belly, flanks, undertail coverts
slides.notes: Walk through Figure 4.3, then describe a robin aloud using only these words.

slides.title: Behavior and habitat
bullets: Robin: run, stop, stare at the ground
Nuthatch: headfirst down the trunk
Turkey Vulture: wings in a V, teetering
Habitat narrows the list but is not a rule
slides.notes: Behavior can be seen before field marks. Flight style links straight back to the wing shapes of Chapter 2.

slides.title: Range, season and proof
bullets: Only Ruby-throated Hummingbirds breed in the East
Many robins stay all winter
Several independent lines of evidence must agree
Rule out look-alikes; keep checkable evidence
slides.notes: Common birds are common. A rare bird needs stronger evidence, which is why eBird flags unusual reports for review.

slides.title: Field guides
bullets: Taxonomic order keeps families together
Plates show plumages; text gives voice and habitat
Range maps: breeding, winter, year-round, migration
Apps give hypotheses, not answers
slides.notes: Have students find the woodpecker pages and the finch pages in their own guide and compare look-alikes on facing pages.

slides.title: Notes and checklists
bullets: Write and sketch before you look at the book
eBird: launched 2002 by Cornell Lab and Audubon
A complete checklist reports every species identified
Complete lists let scientists measure absence and effort
slides.notes: Chapter 8 asks for a full standardized count, so start the habit now with short complete checklists.

slides.title: Summary
bullets: Size and shape give the family
Field marks, named by topography, give the species
Behavior, habitat, range and season test the answer
Notes and complete checklists make it checkable
slides.notes: Before the quiz, describe one bird you saw this week using each of the four steps, in four sentences.

quiz.q: According to the Cornell Lab’s four keys, which should you assess first on an unfamiliar bird?
choices: Its color pattern
Its habitat
Its size and shape
Its song
quiz.explanation: The four keys are size and shape, color pattern, behavior and habitat, in that order. Size and shape work in poor light and usually reveal the family.

quiz.q: A black-and-white woodpecker at a feeder is noticeably longer than a House Sparrow beside it, and its bill is about as long as its head. Which species is it most likely to be?
choices: Hairy Woodpecker
Downy Woodpecker
White-breasted Nuthatch
Red-tailed Hawk
quiz.explanation: Hairy Woodpeckers (18–26 cm) are larger than Downy Woodpeckers (14–17 cm), and their bill is about as long as the head; a Downy’s bill is clearly shorter than its head.

quiz.q: Where on a bird is the malar stripe?
choices: Above the eye
Across the folded wing
On the rump
Running back from the base of the lower mandible, along the side of the throat
quiz.explanation: The malar stripe runs back from the base of the lower bill between the cheek and the throat. The stripe above the eye is the supercilium, and lines across the wing are wing bars.

quiz.q: A male finch has red on its head, breast and rump, a brown back, and brown streaks along its flanks. Which species does this fit?
choices: Purple Finch
House Finch
Northern Cardinal
American Robin
quiz.explanation: Male House Finches have red mostly on the head, breast and rump, with streaked flanks. Male Purple Finches have red washed over the back and wings, and flanks without distinct streaks.

quiz.q: Which flight behavior best separates a soaring Turkey Vulture from a soaring Red-tailed Hawk?
choices: The vulture flaps constantly
The vulture hovers in place
The vulture holds its wings in a shallow V and teeters; the hawk soars on flat wings
The hawk holds its wings in a V; the vulture soars on flat wings
quiz.explanation: Turkey Vultures soar with a dihedral and rock from side to side, rarely flapping. Red-tailed Hawks soar on flat wings.

quiz.q: A hummingbird hovers at a feeder in Ohio in July. Before seeing any field marks, which species is the strong favorite, and why?
choices: Rufous Hummingbird, because it is the most widespread hummingbird
Ruby-throated Hummingbird, because it is the only hummingbird that breeds in eastern North America
Any species is equally likely until you see the throat
Bee Hummingbird, because it is the smallest
quiz.explanation: Range and season make the Ruby-throated Hummingbird the expected species in the East in summer. Field marks then confirm it.

quiz.q: Most North American field guides put the ducks and geese near the front and the songbirds near the back. Why?
choices: They follow the taxonomic order of an official checklist
They are arranged from largest to smallest bird
They are arranged by color
They are arranged alphabetically
quiz.explanation: Guides follow checklist order, which groups related species and families. That is why knowing a bird’s family lets you turn straight to the right pages.

quiz.q: Two birders each visit the same marsh for an hour. One submits a complete checklist without a Marsh Wren; the other submits an incomplete list of only the birds she found interesting, also without a Marsh Wren. What can a researcher conclude?
choices: Both lists show the wren was absent
Neither list says anything about the wren
The incomplete list is more reliable because it is selective
Only the complete list suggests the wren was not detected, because it reports every species identified
quiz.explanation: A complete checklist reports every species the observer identified, so a missing species was probably not detected. An incomplete list may simply have left the wren out.

challenge.title: Ten birds, ten arguments
challenge.prompt: Choose ten photographs of different bird species common in your region from the Cornell Lab’s All About Birds or Macaulay Library, but have a friend pick them and hide the names, or cover the captions yourself. Identify each bird to species. For each one, write out your reasoning using the method of this chapter: size and shape, field marks named by topography, and any clues to behavior, habitat, range or season visible in the photo. Name at least one look-alike for each and the mark that rules it out. Then check your answers and explain any mistakes.
challenge.deliverable: Ten numbered entries, each with your identification, three to five sentences of reasoning, the look-alike you ruled out and how, and a note on whether you were right; then one paragraph on what your mistakes had in common.
rubric: Reasons through size and shape before plumage in most entries
Uses correct topographic terms for the field marks
Names a realistic look-alike for each bird and a specific mark that separates them
Checks answers honestly and explains each error
Draws a general lesson from the pattern of errors

challenge.title: Field notes before the book
challenge.prompt: Find a bird outdoors that you cannot name at once and watch it for at least five minutes. Before opening a guide or app, write full field notes: date, time, place, habitat and weather; size against a reference bird; shape; field marks by topography; behavior; and a rough sketch. Then identify it with a field guide, checking the range map for your area and season. Finally, compare your notes with the guide and list what you noticed, what you missed and what you would look for next time.
challenge.deliverable: Your original field notes (with a typed description of the sketch), your identification with the evidence for it and the look-alikes you excluded, and a reflection of 100 to 200 words.
rubric: Notes were made before consulting the guide and include when, where and habitat
Describes size against a reference bird and shape in specific terms
Names field marks with correct topographic terms
Supports the identification with converging evidence, including range and season, and excludes look-alikes
Reflection identifies specific gaps in observation
